project.name: treetracker-field-data
project.description: Field data service owning raw tree tracking data uploaded from treetracker app devices. Multi-layer MVC-like architecture (Protocol/Service/Model/Repository) over dual PostgreSQL databases, publishing domain events via RabbitMQ.

nodes.languageNotes: Uses Rascal Broker with republish/nack recovery strategies for at-least-once delivery.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to learn what this service does: it owns the raw tree-tracking data that treetracker app devices upload. The document explains the MVC-like multi-layer architecture (Protocol, Service, Model, Repository) that sits on two PostgreSQL databases and publishes domain events through RabbitMQ. Read it first to build the mental map that the rest of the tour fills in.

tour.title: Entry Point and Bootstrap
tour.description: The service starts here. server.js is the process entry point: it loads environment config, starts the HTTP listener on port 3006, and closes the Knex connections on shutdown. It hands off to app.js, which builds the Express application by wiring middleware, Swagger docs, routes, error handling, and the domain event handlers, while config.js exposes the primary and legacy database connection strings that every layer below depends on.

tour.title: Protocol Layer: Routes and Handlers
tour.description: The Protocol layer is the HTTP front door. routes/index.js is a barrel that aggregates every feature router; rawCaptureRoutes.js maps capture URLs to handler functions with async error wrapping. The handler then validates the request against Joi schemas and delegates business work to the service layer, keeping controllers thin. This is the pattern every feature (captures, tracks, sessions, wallets, device config, replay) repeats.
tour.languageLesson: Express routers separate URL-to-handler mapping from request logic. Wrapping async handlers in an error-catching helper forwards rejected promises to the central error middleware, so handlers can 'throw' instead of manually calling next(err).

tour.title: Service Layer: Business Orchestration
tour.description: Building on the handlers from Step 3, the Service layer holds stateless business logic and acts as a factory for domain models. RawCaptureService orchestrates capture creation and rejection across the main and legacy databases using dual transactions, then publishes an event. QueueService wraps RabbitMQ to emit capture-created and capture-rejected messages, while EventHandlerService subscribes to incoming events and processes them inside a transactional session.

tour.title: Domain Model Layer
tour.description: Services create Model objects that carry business state and behavior. RawCapture is the core model: it creates, verifies, and rejects captures and emits a matching domain event for each action. DomainEvent implements the event-sourcing outbox record, and SessionModel represents a capture session. These models raise events rather than talk to the queue directly, which keeps business rules independent of infrastructure.

tour.title: Repository Layer: Data Access
tour.description: Repositories are where all SQL lives, isolating persistence from the models above. BaseRepository is a generic Knex-backed class providing getById, filtered queries, count, update, and create through a recursive where-clause builder; the fan-in analysis ranks it among the most depended-on files in the project. RawCaptureRepository extends this pattern, joining session, wallet-registration, and device-configuration data, while EventRepository adds domain-event insertion and lookup.
tour.languageLesson: A generic base repository centralizes query construction so feature repositories only declare their table and custom joins. This is the Repository pattern: it hides the database driver behind a stable method surface, making the service and model layers testable without a live database.

tour.title: Dual-Database Infrastructure
tour.description: The repositories run on the connection machinery defined here. knex.js constructs two Knex clients, one for the field-data database and one for the legacy treetracker main database, parsing connection strings into SSL-aware objects. BaseSession manages a single Knex connection and its transaction lifecycle (begin, commit, rollback), and Session binds that abstraction to the primary database, which is how services like RawCaptureService coordinate atomic writes.

tour.title: Messaging: RabbitMQ Event Publishing
tour.description: This is the infrastructure behind QueueService from Step 4. RabbitMQ.js wraps the Rascal broker to publish messages and subscribe to queues with retry, republish, and dead-letter handling. The config factory declares the vhosts, exchanges, queues, bindings, publications, and subscriptions for capture events, defining the full messaging topology that carries domain events out of the service and back in for processing.
tour.languageLesson: Rascal is a configuration-driven layer over amqplib: exchanges, queues, and bindings are declared as data rather than imperative setup calls. Dead-letter queues capture messages that repeatedly fail processing, preventing a single poison message from blocking the pipeline.

tour.title: Database Schema and API Contract
tour.description: These artifacts define the shapes the code assumes. The createCaptures migration builds the raw_capture table (image, GPS, field user, status) with supporting indexes, which is the persistence backing the RawCapture model from Step 5. The domainEvents migration creates the domain_event outbox table with yearly range partitions that the event-sourcing flow relies on, and api.json is the OpenAPI 3 contract describing the /captures operations exposed by the Protocol layer.
tour.languageLesson: db-migrate keeps paired up/down SQL files so schema changes stay reversible. Partitioning a high-volume outbox table by year keeps queries and index maintenance fast as the event log grows.

tour.title: Containerization and Kubernetes Deployment
tour.description: With the app understood, see how it ships. The Dockerfile is a single-stage build on node:16-alpine that installs locked npm dependencies and runs the service via the package main entry point from Step 2. The Kubernetes Deployment runs two replicas of the service, and the Kustomize base aggregates the deployment, service, secret, and Ambassador mapping manifests that the development, test, and production overlays extend.
tour.languageLesson: Kustomize layers a base set of manifests with per-environment overlays, so shared config lives once in the base and each environment only patches what differs (replica counts, secrets, hostnames). This avoids duplicating full manifests per environment.

tour.title: CI/CD Pipelines
tour.description: The GitHub Actions workflows automate quality and delivery. The pull-request CI workflow spins up dependencies and runs the test suite on every PR to main, while the build-deploy pipeline runs on push to main, then uses semantic-release to version and publish before promoting the image. Together they gate merges and drive environment promotion without manual steps.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions trigger on 'on' events (pull_request, push), run jobs in parallel, and execute ordered steps within each job. semantic-release reads Conventional Commit messages to decide the next version number automatically.

tour.title: Integration Tests
tour.description: The tour ends where correctness is proven. These Mocha/Chai/Supertest suites exercise the full stack end to end: raw-capture-api.spec.js drives the capture endpoints against a real Postgres database, and events-api.spec.js verifies that domain events publish and get handled correctly through the messaging flow from Step 8. Reading them confirms how every layer you toured fits together under real requests.
